extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness and whether prior art should be disqualified under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), including when references teach away, when an 'obvious-to-try' rationale applies, definitions of common ownership, joint research agreement criteria, effective dates, and examiner procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try rationale for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be shown where the art is choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success — i.e., an invention was "obvious to try."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR: combination obvious-to-try might show obviousness under §103 when a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue known options and success is reasonably expected. However, 'obvious to try' is not the standard where (a) one would vary all parameters or try numerous choices without prior art indicating critical parameters or likely successful choices, or (b) the prior art only gives general guidance suggesting exploration of a promising field (e.g., new technology) without direction. In contrast, obviousness has been found where a reference gives a detailed enabling methodology, suggests modification to produce the claimed invention, and shows reason to expect success (see In re O'Farrell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion/motivation to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggestion or motivation to combine prior art references is an appropriate method to support an obviousness determination, but it is only one of several valid rationales consistent with Graham and KSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may rely on suggestion/motivation to combine among other rationales identified in KSR. See MPEP §2141 and §2143 for additional discussion of permissible rationales and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: References that 'teach away' from the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that "teaches away" from the claimed invention is a significant factor to consider in determining obviousness; the nature of the teaching must be weighed in substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching away can be evidence of nonobviousness, but mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not, by itself, teach away (In re Fulton). A reference criticizing, discrediting, or discouraging the claimed solution may teach away (In re Gurley). Where references teach away from a combination, it is improper to combine them (In re Grasselli). Examiners must assess how strongly a reference discourages the claimed approach and weigh that in the obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom evidences nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceeding contrary to the accepted wisdom or conventional practice in the art can be evidence supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art as a whole suggests a different approach (e.g., lower temperatures, different materials) and the claimed invention goes against that accepted wisdom yet achieves claimed results, that may support nonobviousness (In re Hedges). Known disadvantages in old devices that would discourage pursuit of the new invention are also relevant (United States v. Adams). Examiners should consider the totality of prior art and whether the claimed invention runs counter to accepted practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of KSR across technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles articulated in KSR apply across all fields of technology; KSR is not limited to 'predictable arts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should not withdraw a rejection solely because the invention lies in a technological area ordinarily considered unpredictable (see In re Kubin). The KSR framework can be applied in biotechnology and other areas; examiners must analyze predictability but cannot assume KSR inapplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard for disqualifying prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) provides that subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of section 102 shall not preclude patentability under §103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory disqualification applies only to obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103; it does not disqualify prior art for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections or double-patenting rejections. If subject matter qualifies as prior art under other subsections of 102 (e.g., 102(a) or (b)), it is not disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c). Applicants who assert disqualification must establish it (see MPEP §2146 and §2146.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement conditions for disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), subject matter developed by another and a claimed invention shall be deemed owned by the same person if (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. All three conditions must be satisfied to treat the other's subject matter as commonly owned for §103 purposes. See MPEP §2146.02 and §2156 for related AIA provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective dates and applicability of AIPA and CREATE Act amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments (AIPA 1999 and CREATE Act 2004) changed the scope and effective dates of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c); applicability depends on filing dates and patent grant dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1999 AIPA amendment adding prior art under former 102(e) applied to applications filed on or after November 29, 1999. The CREATE Act (Dec. 10, 2004) made further amendments effective for patents (including reissue patents) granted on or after December 10, 2004, except those subject to the current 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. For reexamination proceedings and reissue applications, examiners must check the patent/application dates to determine which version of §103(c) applies and whether recapture or other doctrines affect claim presentation. See MPEP §§2146, 2146.01, and §2159.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof to establish disqualification of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent applicant or patentee urging that subject matter is disqualified has the burden of establishing that the prior art is disqualified under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent such disqualification, the examiner should make the appropriate rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) applying the prior art. The burden lies on the party asserting disqualification (applicant or patentee), not on the examiner or the defendant in litigation, because evidence of common ownership or other facts may be uniquely available to the applicant/patentee. Examiners should require a statement that common ownership existed 'at the time the invention was made' when that is relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'commonly owned' (100% ownership) and related constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) purposes, 'commonly owned' is intended to mean the subject matter and the claimed invention are entirely or wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) (i.e., 100% ownership) at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either the subject matter or claimed invention was owned less than 100% by the same entity(ies) at the relevant time, common ownership does not exist. For jointly-owned inventions, the reference must have been owned by (or subject to an obligation of assignment to) the same entities that owned the application at the time of the later invention. Licenses that retain basic ownership rights do not defeat ownership. The question is fact-specific and requires evidence of legal ownership or enforceable obligation to assign — moral or unenforceable obligations are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required statements, disclosures, and duty of candor to establish disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish disqualification under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), parties must provide statements/disclosures demonstrating common ownership or compliance with joint research agreement conditions (e.g., naming parties and invention dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere shared assignee is not sufficient; there must be a statement that common ownership existed 'at the time the invention was made.' Applicants have an obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates and to explain lack of common ownership when relevant. For joint research agreement disqualification, the application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of parties to the agreement. See MPEP §§2146.02–2146.03 for procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue, reexamination, and recapture considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue and reexamination proceedings have special considerations: recapture doctrine and effective-date rules may limit use of amended §103(c) changes to avoid prior rejections or to present claims in reissue applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a patent was granted prior to Dec. 10, 2004 or applications were filed before Nov. 29, 1999, the specific applicable amendments vary; in some reissue scenarios, recapture may prevent presentation of claims amended/cancelled to overcome a previous §103 rejection even if subject matter might now be disqualified. Examiners should consult the Office of Patent Legal Administration via Technology Center Quality Assurance Specialist when such situations arise. See MPEP §§2146.01–2146.03 and §§804, 1490 for related practice.
